feedback: If a learner evaporates first and ends with dry salt crystallised through the sand, don't just correct the order — ask: 'Which of these is dissolved in the water and which is just mixed in but not dissolved?' Rebuild the plan from insoluble vs dissolved, and point out they would now have to add water and begin again.

If a learner expects the filter to catch the salt too, demonstrate safely by evaporating a small drop of the filtrate to leave a tiny visible salt residue: the salt passed straight through, so filters catch undissolved bits, not dissolved substances. Reconnect to what dissolving means. (Do not taste lab substances.)

If a learner correctly executes filter-then-evaporate but explains it only as a remembered recipe, prompt: 'What is different about sand and salt that lets us use these two steps?' so the justification rests on solubility.
activities.intendedInsight: The order matters because each method depends on a specific property difference: the insoluble sand must be filtered out first. If the water is evaporated too early, the dissolved salt crystallises among the sand grains, leaving a dry mixture with no simple way to separate the two solids — you would have to re-dissolve and start over, wasting the step. Method choice follows from properties, not memory.
learnerActions: Start with one beaker holding sand + salt + water and the goal: recover a clean, dry pile of sand AND a clean, dry pile of salt, separated from each other.
Before acting, tag each component with its relevant property: sand = insoluble solid, salt = dissolved (soluble) solid, water = liquid.
Choose an order of techniques from available stations/apparatus (sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet) and carry it out.
Filter first: observe that the insoluble sand stays on the filter paper while the salty water passes through; rinse and dry the sand.

Then evaporate the filtered salt-water: observe the water level falling as the water leaves as invisible water vapour (any visible 'steam' is tiny droplets formed as the vapour cools), and salt crystals remaining behind once the water has gone.

Deliberately try the wrong order (evaporate before filtering) and observe the result: the water leaves and you are back to a dry sand-and-salt mixture with the salt crystallised among the grains — there is no simple DRY way to separate them, so you would have to add water again and start over.
State, for each step, which property difference it exploits.
activities.title: Plan an ordered separation for sand + salt + water

feedback: If a learner picks a method by recall of a past activity rather than the property, ask: 'What is different about these two substances that we can take advantage of?' so the choice is driven by magnetism, solubility, or particle size.
Confirm when a learner correctly links iron filings + sand to a magnet and can say why the magnet works on iron but not sand.
activities.intendedInsight: A separation method is chosen because of a specific property difference between components; the same reasoning transfers to any mixture, so the learner is not bound to one memorised sequence.
learnerActions: Face a different mixture, e.g. iron filings mixed with sand, and decide how to separate it.
Name the property difference being exploited (here, magnetism: iron is magnetic, sand is not) and choose the matching method (a magnet).
Try other new mixtures (e.g. gravel + sand needing a sieve for particle size; a dissolved solid needing evaporation) and justify each method by the property difference.
Explain why a method would fail if the property it relies on were absent (e.g. a magnet does nothing for two non-magnetic solids).
activities.title: Transfer: choose a method for a new mixture by its property

feedback: If a learner says the sieve and filter are the same, contrast them: a sieve separates by particle size (large bits caught, small bits through), while a filter separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
If a learner says evaporating destroys the salt, clarify that the water leaves as vapour and the dissolved solid stays behind.
activities.intendedInsight: Each separation tool exploits one property difference, and knowing which property each relies on is what makes it possible to plan a correct sequence.
learnerActions: Study each piece of apparatus — sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet — and state what it separates (large bits from small; insoluble solid from liquid; dissolved solid from solution; magnetic from non-magnetic).
For each, name the property that makes it work and sketch or label where each component ends up.
Link each tool back to the mixtures it would suit.
activities.title: Apparatus reference: what each tool separates and why
